metadata.note: Passenger rail at Ames, Iowa -- three separate operations, none of which was previously anywhere in this repo (nothing existed within 43 km of the city). (1) The Chicago and North Western main line, which is why Ames exists at all: the Cedar Rapids and Missouri River Rail Road reached Nevada on July 4 1864, the C&NW platted and named Ames that December, Boone followed in 1865 and Council Bluffs in January 1867, making this the first railroad from Chicago to the Missouri River and the eastern approach to the transcontinental route. Union Pacific's City streamliners used it to reach Chicago until October 1955; the Kate Shelley 400 then ran Chicago-Boone through Ames until it was cut back east of the city in 1956. (2) The Ames and College Railway, 'the Dinkey', a steam dummy line from downtown to the Iowa Agricultural College campus, July 4 1891 to 1907. (3) The Fort Dodge, Des Moines and Southern, which bought the Dinkey in 1906, electrified it in 1907 and ran Ames streetcars until September 1929, and which linked Ames to Iowa's longest interurban by a branch north from Kelley, passenger service on that branch ending in late 1928. Ames has had no passenger train since; Amtrak's California Zephyr crosses Iowa about a hundred miles south.
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap via Overpass API (maps.mail.ru mirror). C&NW main: ways with old_railway_operator=C&NW over bbox 41.20,-96.20,42.40,-90.10, corridor-weighted Dijkstra Clinton to Council Bluffs through the documented station towns, 3,058-point raw path simplified at 30 m to 256 points. Ames-Kelley: railway=abandoned ways over bbox 41.90,-93.80,42.10,-93.45. Dinkey: shortest path over OSM highway=* ways in downtown Ames and on campus, weighted toward the streets the sources name.
Nominatim / published coordinates for the station towns and for the Hub, Wheatsfield Cooperative and Main Street at Duff Avenue.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: THE BIG ONE: the date the last passenger train called at Ames. The named train left the route in 1956 and the surviving C&NW trains 1 and 2 were truncated to Clinton by 1957, but whether an unnamed local kept serving Ames into the 1960s was not established. The C&NW features are drawn to 1956 because that is the last year the sources put a scheduled passenger train at Ames -- if evidence of later service turns up, the end year should move, and the same applies to the Boone-Council Bluffs half of the route, for which no separate discontinuance date was found at all. Three of the sources cited here are Ames History Museum pages that could not be fetched directly -- their content reached this file through search-engine summaries of them, so the details attributed to them deserve a direct check. The 1907-1926 versus 1907-1929 conflict over the Ames streetcar span is unresolved; 1929 is drawn. Every headway_min in this layer is an estimate and no timetable of any era was consulted. mode='interurban' on the Kelley branch follows existing files in data/ but is not in the list of mode values documented in CLAUDE.md.

properties.line: Chicago and North Western: Clinton – Boone
properties.speed_source: Estimated for 1860s steam operation. No timetable consulted.
properties.geometry_quality: Fully real-traced from OpenStreetMap, no straight-line bridging over 60 m anywhere. The path runs 309.9 km on the UP Clinton Subdivision, 137.7 km on the Boone Subdivision, 49.3 km on the UP Boone Subdivision and 32.8 km on the UP Omaha Subdivision -- every one of them tagged old_railway_operator=C&NW -- plus short connections at Cedar Rapids, Blair and the Council Bluffs approach, and 820 m over the disused Kate Shelley High Bridge at Boone. Traced 342.8 miles Clinton to Council Bluffs; the Clinton-to-Boone portion measures 198.3 miles against a documented 203 (the Kate Shelley 400's 340-mile Chicago-Boone run less the 137 miles Chicago-Clinton). Towns on the route fall close to the trace: Nevada 0.36 km, Ames 1.07, Boone 0.62, Carroll 0.25, Denison 0.98, Missouri Valley 0.17, Council Bluffs 0.09, Marshalltown 0.69, Clinton 0.89, Cedar Rapids 3.98 (the trace skirts the city centre, which is where the centroid sits). No reversals over 120 degrees. ERA CAVEAT: this is today's Union Pacific alignment. The Kate Shelley High Bridge it crosses at Boone is the 1901 structure, so for the 1864-1901 years the drawn line is a later alignment than its own era at that crossing; the pre-1901 crossing has not been traced. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 1 ruled segment totalling 11 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: The Cedar Rapids and Missouri River Rail Road pushed west from Cedar Rapids, reaching Marshalltown in 1862, State Center in 1863, Nevada by July 4 1864 and Boone in 1865. It was consolidated with the Chicago and North Western in June 1864 and worked as part of that system from then on, which is why the whole line is drawn in C&NW colours rather than split. Ames itself was created by this railroad: the town was laid out in December 1864 and named for John Blair, the C&NW president. This feature stops at Boone because the line did -- Council Bluffs was not reached until January 1867. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: Marshalltown 1862, State Center 1863, Nevada July 4 1864, Boone 1865, the June 1864 consolidation with the C&NW, and the December 1864 platting and naming of Ames are from the Ames History Museum's C&NW page and the Cedar Rapids and Missouri River Railroad article; headway and speed are unsourced estimates.

properties.line: Chicago and North Western: Clinton – Council Bluffs
properties.speed_source: Derived from the Kate Shelley 400's 340 miles Chicago to Boone in about 5 1/2 hours (about 62 mph) and reduced to reflect that most of the drawn span is pre-streamliner steam operation, which was slower. A single figure across 1867-1956 is a compromise, not a measurement.

segments.note: In January 1867 this became the first railroad to reach Council Bluffs from Chicago, meeting the Union Pacific across the Missouri at Omaha -- the eastern end of the first transcontinental railroad. That made Ames a stop on a genuine transcontinental corridor rather than a branch town. Union Pacific's City streamliners -- City of Los Angeles, City of San Francisco, City of Portland, City of Denver -- ran over this line between Omaha and Chicago until October 1955, when UP moved them to the Milwaukee Road. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the January 1867 arrival at Council Bluffs as the first railroad from Chicago, and the October 1955 transfer of the UP City streamliners to the Milwaukee Road, are from the Cedar Rapids and Missouri River Railroad article and the Kate Shelley 400 sources; headway and speed are estimates.

segments.note: With the City streamliners gone, the C&NW put on the Kate Shelley 400 in October 1955, trains 1 and 2, Chicago to Boone via Ames, 340 miles in about 5 1/2 hours. It was cut back to Cedar Rapids in 1956 -- east of Ames -- and to Clinton in 1957. THE DRAWN YEARS END HERE BECAUSE THE SOURCING DOES: 1956 is the last year this route can be shown carrying a scheduled passenger train at Ames. The name was dropped July 23 1963 and unnamed trains 1 and 2 ran until Amtrak on May 1 1971, but only over the Chicago-Clinton stub, nowhere near Ames. Whether any unnamed local kept calling at Ames after 1956 was not established -- see not_yet_sourced. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the October 1955 introduction of the Kate Shelley 400 as trains 1 and 2, the 340 miles in about 5 1/2 hours, the 1956 cutback to Cedar Rapids and 1957 to Clinton, the July 23 1963 dropping of the name and the May 1 1971 end of the unnamed trains are from the Kate Shelley 400 article and American-Rails; headway and speed are estimates.

properties.line: Ames and College Railway: the Dinkey
properties.speed_source: Estimated for a street-running steam dummy over 2.4 miles. No timetable consulted.
properties.geometry_quality: APPROXIMATION, and the weakest geometry in this layer: the Dinkey was street trackage that was lifted from Main Street in August 1930, so nothing of it survives to trace. This is a shortest-path route over today's Ames street grid, weighted toward the three streets the sources actually name, between three documented anchors: the downtown terminus at Main Street and Duff Avenue (by the power plant, with the car barn just east of Duff near the C&NW depot), the crossing of the C&NW by what is now Wheatsfield Cooperative on Northwestern Avenue, and the campus terminal at the Hub. It runs Main Street - Northwestern Avenue - 5th Street - 6th Street and then onto campus by Beach Road, Union Drive and Morrill Road, 2.40 miles. The named streets (Main, Fifth, the Wheatsfield crossing, the Hub) are sourced; the campus approach west of 6th Street is NOT -- it is a plausible modern-street path, not a documented alignment. Treat the western third as indicative only.

segments.note: A joint venture of the city of Ames and the Iowa Agricultural College, opened July 4 1891 to connect downtown with the campus two miles west. RULE 5 NOTE: it was originally proposed as a horse-car railway, and the franchise was granted only on condition that it use engine power instead of animal power -- so it ran a four-wheel steam dummy from its first day and there is no animal-traction era to exclude here. The name probably comes from the size of the engine, or from 'donkey' engine. Sold to the Fort Dodge, Des Moines and Southern in 1906-07 and replaced with electric streetcars. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the July 4 1891 opening, the joint city-college venture, the rejected horse-car proposal and the engine-power condition, the four-wheel steam dummy, the Main Street and Duff Avenue terminus, the Fifth Street running, the C&NW crossing at what is now Wheatsfield Cooperative, the campus terminal at the Hub, and the sale to the FDDM&S are from the Ames History Museum's Dinkey page and the Iowa State campus-buildings history; headway and speed are unsourced estimates.

properties.company: Fort Dodge, Des Moines and Southern Railway
properties.line: Fort Dodge, Des Moines and Southern: Ames – Iowa State College
properties.speed_source: Estimated for a city electric streetcar over 2.4 miles. No timetable consulted.
properties.geometry_quality: APPROXIMATION, and the weakest geometry in this layer: the Dinkey was street trackage that was lifted from Main Street in August 1930, so nothing of it survives to trace. This is a shortest-path route over today's Ames street grid, weighted toward the three streets the sources actually name, between three documented anchors: the downtown terminus at Main Street and Duff Avenue (by the power plant, with the car barn just east of Duff near the C&NW depot), the crossing of the C&NW by what is now Wheatsfield Cooperative on Northwestern Avenue, and the campus terminal at the Hub. segments.note: The FDDM&S bought the Ames and College Railway on May 1 1906 and in 1907 replaced the steam Dinkey with electric streetcars over the same downtown-to-campus route. The railroad started a competing bus service of its own between Ames and Des Moines on August 24 1925, six trips each way; in July 1929 it got permission to suspend streetcars for the summer vacation, and in September 1929 announced they would not resume. The Main Street track was lifted in August 1930. SOURCE CONFLICT: one account gives the Ames streetcar span as 1907 to 1926, which does not fit the 1929 suspension detail; 1929 is drawn here. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the May 1 1906 purchase of the Ames and College Railway, the 1907 electrification, the August 24 1925 start of the competing bus service, the July 1929 summer suspension, the September 1929 announcement that service would not resume, and the August 1930 track removal are from the Ames History Museum FDDM&S page and Iowa DOT's Ames transit history; the conflicting 1907-1926 span comes from the same body of sources. Headway and speed are unsourced estimates.

properties.company: Fort Dodge, Des Moines and Southern Railway
properties.line: Fort Dodge, Des Moines and Southern: Ames – Kelley
properties.speed_source: Estimated for a 1,200-volt DC interurban branch. No timetable consulted.
properties.geometry_quality: Mostly real-traced: 5.84 miles from the Hub on the Iowa State campus south to Kelley, of which 1.91 km (1.19 mi) at the Ames end is a STRAIGHT-LINE APPROXIMATION and the remaining 4.65 miles follow railway=abandoned ways in OpenStreetMap, two of them tagged old_railway_operator='Fort Dodge, Des Moines and Southern Railway'. The straight leg exists because the surviving abandoned alignment stops at 42.0097/-93.6493, south of the built-up city, and no source consulted gives the interurban's exact approach to its Ames terminal; it is drawn to the campus Hub so the branch meets the city line rather than ending in a field. The southern end stops 0.41 km east of Kelley village centre -- that is where the traced alignment runs out, apparently at the junction with the FDDM&S main rather than in the village itself, and it has not been confirmed against a period map. One out-and-back spike at the Kelley end was removed; no turn on the finished line exceeds 100 degrees.

segments.note: Ames was not on the FDDM&S main line, which ran Des Moines - Ankeny - Hope - Fort Dodge, 85 miles; it was reached by this branch north from Kelley, and full service over the system opened November 4 1907. This is the connection that put Ames on Iowa's longest interurban and gave it electric cars through to Des Moines and Fort Dodge. Interurban passenger service between Ames and Kelley was discontinued in late 1928, after the company had put its own competing buses on the road; passenger service on the FDDM&S generally ended in the mid-1950s alongside dieselization, and the C&NW acquired the railroad in 1968 -- neither of which is drawn here, because neither applies to this branch. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the Des Moines - Ankeny - Hope - Fort Dodge main line and the branch to Ames from Kelley, the November 4 1907 opening of full service, and the late-1928 end of Ames-Kelley interurban passenger service are from American-Rails' FDDM&S history and the Ames History Museum FDDM&S page; headway and speed are unsourced estimates.
